Ikegwu et al. developed a fast computational framework for the design of solvent- based plastic recycling processes, integrated techno-economic and life cycle assessment, and leveraged it to screen 1,000 green solvents to separate post-industrial multilayered films (Ikegwu, Munguía-López, et al., 2025; Ikegwu, Zhou, et al., 2025). As part of Subtask 3.1.2, we used the aforementioned database of Subtask 3.1.1 to build a digital tool based on large language models (LLMs) that provides recommendations on how to best route diverse feedstocks based on their characteristics. The digital tool also provides detailed recommendations on solvents that can be used to recycle specific layers in STRAP. We are currently in the process of putting together a manuscript based on this. In the context of the STRAP process, we have also developed machine learning models for predicting solubility and we have found that such models can achieve high accuracy. The results are part of Subtask 3.1.3. As part of this task we have also developed new machine learning methodologies to visualize large chemical spaces that we are using for identifying best solvents to separate contaminants such as PFAS from plastic waste. Under Task 4.1, we sought to evaluate the viability of recycling and upcycling infrastructure under realistic markets, technological performances, and policy conditions. For example, as part of Subtask 4.1.1, Subtask 4.1.2, and Subtask 4.1.3, Olafasakin et al. established economic and environmental benchmarks for standalone single-stream municipal recovery facilities (Olafasakin, Ma, Bradshaw, et al., 2023). Comparative TEA/LCA work by Olafasakin et al. quantified tradeoffs between conventional pyrolysis and thermal oxo-degradation for producing fuels and chemicals from waste plastics, with and without hydrocracking (Olafasakin, Ma, Zavala, et al., 2023). Hydrocracking longer- chain hydrocarbons to more valuable naphtha and diesel products can significantly increase the revenue from 28 to 72 million USD for a facility processing 250 tons of waste HDPE/day. However, it also increases the fixed capital investment from 33 to 244 million USD. Through rigorous techno-economic analysis, we identified that pathways without hydrocracking had greater net present values and were hence more economically viable. The model codes and databases for this study are freely available at https://github.com/lumedee007/TOD-CPY-TEA-LCA. As another example, the work of Erickson et al. studied the deployment of a pyrolysis based infrastructure for processing plastic waste under many scenarios that explore transportation costs, market conditions, targets for recovery of plastics, and technology performance; this study also compared benefits of upcycling relative to landfilling and incineration (Erickson et al., 2024). Our results demonstrate that the infrastructure could generate a market of nearly 20 billion USD per year (a measure of total economic surplus) which provides opportunities for residents to be compensated for recycling plastic. Our analysis also indicates that the infrastructure can achieve a plastic-to-plastic degree of circularity of 34% relative to residential plastic waste production and leads to significant environmental benefits over alternative waste disposal methods, including 69%–75% lower greenhouse gas emissions than waste-to-energy systems and 38 million tons of avoided landfill waste per year.
